headline: Tech stocks surge on strong Alphabet and Microsoft momentum, but all eyes on next week's RBA rate decision as all four major banks now tip a hike.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI bounced strongly today on the ASX, riding broader optimism around AI stocks. No specific catalyst for the ETF itself, but the global AI theme remains hot — UK parliament is summoning the big AI labs for a safety hearing, and regulatory momentum is building worldwide. Still in the red overall (-9.25% on total investment), but today's session was a solid step in the right direction.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two jumped last night on continued GTA 6 excitement — Rockstar Games released a new modding policy ahead of the game's launch, signalling the release is getting closer. Fan engagement is at a fever pitch with interactive maps of the game world already circulating online. Still down 9.6% overall, but GTA 6 buzz continues to be the key catalyst to watch.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Alphabet had a strong night last night, rising 1.88%. Analysts lifted their earnings estimates following strong Q2 2026 figures, and the launch of Gemini 3.8 Live is putting Google's enterprise AI revenue story front and centre. Stock is holding near record levels — up 14.1% on your total investment.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft climbed 1.59% last night as investors look ahead to Q1 revenue results. The market is broadly bullish on Microsoft's AI monetisation story through Copilot and Azure. Up 13.2% on your total investment — a solid long-term hold.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS had a good session today on the ASX, tracking last night's strong US market performance. The S&P 500 and NASDAQ both surged, lifting this broad US market ETF. Up 3.89% on total investment — doing its job as a diversified US exposure.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE nudged higher today. The WEF flagged India as one of the strongest growth outlooks globally, which is positive for emerging markets broadly. Virtually breakeven on your total investment — a slow but steady long-term play.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG edged up today, tracking global market gains. No specific news, just the broad market tailwind. Essentially flat on your total investment — this is a set-and-forget long-term holding doing exactly what it should.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS was dead flat today — no movement at all. Lithium carbonate prices continue their weak trend with multiple bearish factors converging, including oversupply concerns. This is your biggest loss position at -38.7% on total investment. The long-term lithium demand story (EVs, batteries) is intact, but the commodity cycle is firmly in a down phase right now.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike next week — all four major banks now agree
watch_today.detail: CBA, ANZ, NAB and Westpac all now forecast the RBA will lift interest rates at next Tuesday's meeting. The RBA Governor has said 'heat' needs to be taken out of the job market. This will push mortgage rates higher for millions of Australians. For your portfolio, a rate hike tends to weigh on growth stocks and property — keep an eye on your VDHG and VGE positions which have some interest rate sensitivity.

watch_today.title: TTWO — Hold, GTA 6 hype building
watch_today.detail: Take-Two is still down 9.6% on your total investment, but the GTA 6 release is getting closer — Rockstar just published a new modding policy, fan maps of the game world are going viral, and buzz is at an all-time high. The long-term thesis here is entirely GTA 6. Sit tight — this is a pre-launch hype cycle and the real test is the game's actual release. Don't sell into weakness now.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Hold, but lithium pain continues
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals is your biggest loser at -38.7% and went nowhere today. Lithium carbonate prices are still falling with multiple bearish factors piling on — oversupply, weak Chinese EV demand signals. The long-term EV battery demand story is still real, but the commodity cycle could stay ugly for a while yet. Don't sell at these lows — you'd be locking in a big loss. Hold and be patient.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — Hold, AI regulation headwinds emerging
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF bounced 2.76% today, which is great. But watch this space — the UK parliament is hauling in Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic for a safety hearing, and Australia has backed tougher global AI regulation. Increased regulation could slow AI deployment and weigh on AI-exposed stocks. Nothing to act on now, but worth monitoring as this regulatory story develops.

watch_today.title: Oil drops nearly 6% — watch for flow-on effects
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) fell a sharp 5.77% last night to $90.25 a barrel. That's a big single-day move, likely linked to easing Middle East risk premium after Trump reportedly called off airstrikes at the last minute. Cheaper oil is generally good for the broader economy (lower inflation, cheaper transport costs) but is worth monitoring given the ongoing Middle East tensions.

watch_today.title: GOOG — Hold, analysts lifting targets
watch_today.detail: Alphabet is up 14.1% on your investment and analysts are actively raising their earnings forecasts on the back of strong Q2 results and Gemini 3.8 momentum. Nothing to do here — this is a long-term hold firing on all cylinders.

world.summary: The Middle East conflict dominates global headlines as Iran claims the US was planning a new bombing campaign, Trump called off airstrikes at the last minute, and the Houthis moved to seize strategic terrain. Meanwhile the WEF has warned the conflict is the single biggest threat to the global economy, and the US is planning a $5 billion reconstruction fund.

stories.title: Middle East on the brink: Iran claims US planned bombing campaign, Houthis seize ground
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has publicly claimed the US was planning to renew its bombing campaign in the region, dramatically raising tensions. In a wild twist, Trump reportedly called off US airstrikes at the last minute — and the Houthis in Yemen immediately moved to seize strategic terrain, sensing the window of opportunity. This is a fast-moving, dangerous situation. For everyday Australians, the key risk is oil price spikes and global economic disruption if the conflict widens further.

stories.title: WEF: Middle East conflict is the biggest single threat to the global economy
stories.why_it_matters: The World Economic Forum's chief economists have flagged the widening Middle East war as the number one risk to global growth right now. While the overall economic outlook is improving, uncertainty remains very high. For investors, this means continued volatility in oil prices, potential supply chain disruptions, and risk-off moves in global sharemarkets if the conflict escalates.

stories.title: US plans $5 billion Middle East reconstruction fund
stories.why_it_matters: The US is reportedly planning a $5 billion reconstruction fund for the Middle East in the wake of the Iran conflict. This signals Washington is thinking about a post-war phase, but also reflects the enormous scale of damage already done. For global markets, reconstruction spending of this scale could be a meaningful economic stimulus — though it also confirms the conflict has been severe.

stories.title: Saudi Arabia's new defence pact faces a major test as war widens
stories.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia recently signed a new defence partnership, but the widening war in the region is now putting that pact under serious pressure. Saudi Arabia's stability is crucial to global oil supplies — if it gets drawn deeper into the conflict, energy markets could face major disruption. Australia, as a big energy importer, would feel higher petrol and gas prices quickly.

stories.title: US midterm elections 40 days away — Trump's biggest campaign target is Biden
stories.why_it_matters: With US midterm elections just 40 days away, Trump has mentioned Joe Biden nearly 900 times on the campaign trail — making him the central villain of his pitch to voters even though Biden is no longer president. Analysts warn Trump risks 'lame duck' status early if Republicans underperform. US political stability matters for markets globally — a messy midterm result could add to uncertainty already building around the Middle East conflict.

markets.summary: A cracking night on Wall Street last night — the NASDAQ surged 2.26% and the S&P 500 gained 1.49%, driven by strength in tech. The ASX had a modest follow-through today, up just 0.3%. The big market surprise was a near-6% crash in oil prices, while gold was essentially flat. The Aussie dollar slipped slightly against the USD.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Modest gain today — tech tailwinds from Wall Street didn't fully flow through.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Strong night last night — broad US market gains driven by tech optimism.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Best performer last night — big tech and AI stocks led the charge.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Sharp drop — Trump reportedly called off Middle East airstrikes, easing the risk premium in oil.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Essentially flat — no major moves despite Middle East tensions.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar barely moved — slight dip ahead of next week's expected RBA rate hike.

politics.summary: The big domestic story is a potential interest rate hike next week — all four major banks have now changed their forecasts and are calling for the RBA to lift rates at its Tuesday meeting. The RBA Governor's own comments have added fuel to the fire, saying the job market needs to cool down.

stories.title: All four major banks now tipping an RBA rate hike next Tuesday
stories.why_it_matters: CBA and ANZ have joined NAB and Westpac in forecasting the RBA will raise interest rates at next Tuesday's board meeting — a significant shift for CBA and ANZ, who had previously been more cautious. The RBA Governor reinforced this view today, saying 'heat' needs to be taken out of the job market. For anyone with a variable-rate mortgage, this means another repayment increase is likely coming. It also puts upward pressure on the Australian dollar and could weigh on consumer spending.

stories.title: RBA Governor signals rate rise needed to cool hot jobs market
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA Governor has explicitly said the labour market still has too much heat and rates need to rise further to bring inflation back to target. This is the clearest signal yet from the RBA itself — not just from bank economists — that a hike is coming. Employment data remains strong, which means the RBA feels it has room to tighten without crashing the economy. Everyday Australians with mortgages should be prepared.

stories.title: Major banks shock the market with double rate hike forecasts
stories.why_it_matters: Some forecasters are now flagging the possibility of not just one but two rate hikes before Christmas. Realestate.com.au reports the major banks' sudden pivot has shocked the property market, with borrowers scrambling to check their repayment buffers. A double hike scenario would add hundreds of dollars per month to a typical $600,000 mortgage. Property prices in Sydney and Melbourne could come under renewed pressure if this eventuates.

ai.summary: AI regulation is the dominant theme today — the UK parliament has summoned the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic for a safety hearing, Australia has backed tougher global AI rules, and a new antitrust lawsuit has been filed against the big AI labs alleging they secretly agreed to slow AI development.

stories.title: UK parliament summons Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic for AI safety hearing
stories.why_it_matters: The UK's parliamentary Business Committee has formally invited the CEOs of Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic to appear before MPs amid growing concerns about AI safety risks. This is a significant escalation — governments are no longer just talking about regulation, they're demanding answers directly from the companies building the most powerful AI systems in the world. For investors in Google (GOOG) and the GXAI ETF, regulatory scrutiny is a real headwind that could slow product deployment and increase compliance costs.

stories.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI sued over alleged secret pact to slow AI development
stories.why_it_matters: A major antitrust lawsuit has been filed against OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Elon Musk's xAI, alleging the companies secretly agreed to slow down AI development — essentially colluding to limit competition rather than racing ahead. This is a serious allegation: if proven, it could mean big fines and forced changes to how these companies operate. It's also a strange accusation given how fast AI has been moving — the case will be fascinating to watch.

stories.title: Australia backs push for tougher global AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Australia has officially backed an international push for stricter AI regulation, joining a growing coalition of governments calling for a global governance body to manage AI risks. The AFR reports this is framed as a 'risk to safety and security' — covering everything from deepfakes to autonomous weapons to job displacement. For Australian businesses and tech investors, this signals that AI-related compliance requirements are coming, likely within the next few years.

stories.title: Google launches Gemini 3.8 Live — enterprise AI revenue now in focus
stories.why_it_matters: Google has launched Gemini 3.8 Live, its latest AI model, with a particular focus on enterprise customers — businesses paying for AI tools built into Google's cloud and productivity products. Analysts are now watching closely to see how much new revenue this actually generates, with earnings estimates being lifted off the back of strong Q2 results. For GOOG holders, this is the key question for the next 12 months: can Google turn its AI leadership into real dollars?

sport.summary: NRL Finals Week 3 is set — Dolphins host the Roosters on Friday night at Suncorp, and Panthers face the Knights on Sunday. There's big team news with a major Walker move at the Roosters, while four players including DCE were fined by the judiciary after Finals Week 2. AFL Grand Final week is also heating up with Brownlow Medal results, draft rankings and scalping warnings.

stories.title: Roosters make major Walker move ahead of Finals Week 3 prelim
stories.why_it_matters: The Roosters have made a major positional move involving Walker ahead of their do-or-die prelim final against the Dolphins on Friday at Suncorp Stadium. Fox Sports reports this Walker call could make NRL history, while Penrith's decision to name Cleary is described as 'obvious' — the Panthers are widely expected to field their best side for the Knights clash on Sunday. Team tips are out now for both prelim finals.

stories.title: NRL Judiciary: DCE among four players fined after Finals Week 2
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL Judiciary handed down its rulings from Finals Week 2, with Daly Cherry-Evans (DCE) among four players copping fines. No suspensions were handed down from the results, meaning all four should be available for their respective clubs heading into the prelim finals this weekend.

stories.title: Penrith vs Newtown — NSW Cup Grand Final
stories.why_it_matters: While the NRL first-grade prelims dominate attention, the NSW Cup Grand Final is also being played between Penrith and Newtown — a big club football occasion that could showcase future NRL stars for both sides.

stories.title: AFL Grand Final week: Brownlow results, scalping warnings and draft rankings
stories.why_it_matters: AFL Grand Final week is in full swing. The Brownlow Medal votes are in — afl.com.au has a full breakdown of total votes, first-time winners and biggest shocks by club. The Victorian government's consumer affairs department is also warning fans about ticket scalping ahead of Grand Final day. And Richmond FC has published its list of top 2026 draft prospects, with September rankings updated for the upcoming national draft.
